review_basis: Original full-resolution numbered Module 13 WebP slides 01-04 individually inspected; source examples, visible arrows, labels, limitations and decisions used for narration.
part_title: Context Engineering, Agents, MCP Tools and Memory

scenes.title: Context engineering
scenes.visual_overview: A five-stage customer-support architecture builds a bounded context from trusted current evidence, tools and conversation state before the foundation model answers.
visual_walkthrough: Request with laptop-refund question, order ID and prior turn
Bedrock Knowledge Bases semantic search and filter to current policy
Five elements in bounded context: system instruction, user prompt, retrieved evidence, tool results and memory
Bedrock foundation model uses curated input
Grounded answer cites refund policy and order record; worked example and exam cue
scenes.visual_example: A customer bought a laptop 20 days ago; a 30-day return policy and verified order-delivery details support an eligible refund answer with citations [1] and [2].
scenes.visual_synthesis: Reliable context engineering selects relevant authorized evidence; it does not simply dump all documents into a prompt.
scenes.narration: This architecture shows how a support assistant answers a refund question using the right evidence, rather than guessing from the model's general knowledge. Start at the blue request panel. The customer asks whether a laptop bought twenty days ago can be refunded. The conversation also identifies the customer and order. Next, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases performs semantic search, meaning it looks for relevant meaning, and filters results to the latest trusted refund policy. Beside it, the three inputs labelled retrieved evidence, tool results and memory show different sources: policy text, verified order information and relevant conversation state. Follow their arrows into the bounded context window. The five rows combine system instructions, the user's question, current policy, trusted order data and just the memory needed for this request. A context window is the amount of input the model can consider; more text is not necessarily better. In the purple panel, the Bedrock foundation model generates a response from that curated material. The green answer concludes the return is eligible because the pictured example combines a thirty-day policy with a twenty-day-old delivery, and it cites both the policy and order record. The lower strip repeats the journey from question to evidence to answer. The exam decision is to select relevant, current, authorized context and make the conclusion verifiable, not to paste an entire knowledge base into every request.

scenes.title: Agents and workflows
scenes.visual_overview: A side-by-side comparison distinguishes deterministic workflows, single dynamic agents and supervisors coordinating specialized agents.
visual_walkthrough: Left fixed classify–retrieve–draft–human review chain
Center goal–plan–call tool–observe–iterate agent loop
Right supervisor delegates research and validation then combines results
Market research brief contrasts fixed workflow and dynamic agent
Exam cue chooses predictable rules versus dynamic multi-step decisions
scenes.visual_example: A market-research brief follows classify/retrieve/draft/review when steps are fixed; an agent can plan sources, search, analyze findings, and revise when new competitor information appears.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use simple workflows when steps are stable, agents when reasoning and tool selection must adapt, and supervisors only when specialist coordination justifies added complexity.
scenes.narration: This slide compares three ways to automate a task; the columns are alternatives, not steps every project must follow. On the left, a deterministic workflow performs the same predictable sequence: classify a request, retrieve data, draft a response and ask a person to review it. It is easier to test when the rules are known. In the middle, the AI agent works in a loop. It understands a goal, plans what to do, calls an allowed tool, observes the result and iterates until the goal is reached or a stopping rule applies. Here a tool might be a search or a business application. On the right, the supervisor coordinates specialized research and validation agents, then combines their outputs. This adds capability but also more handoffs and oversight. Now look at the market-research example along the bottom. The fixed approach collects company and industry reports before an analyst approves a structured brief. The dynamic approach starts with a broader goal, searches and analyzes sources, then may revise the plan when it discovers a missing competitor. The supervisory approach would separate gathering evidence from checking its accuracy. The exam cue on the right summarizes the decision: predictable rules favor a workflow; changing multi-step goals can justify an agent. Human review and permission controls still matter whichever approach you choose.

scenes.title: MCP and tool connections
scenes.visual_overview: An agent application's MCP client discovers defined tools on an MCP server and uses scoped permissions to reach external CRM or search APIs.
visual_walkthrough: User request for latest Acme Corp CRM opportunity enters agent application
Client discovers tool schema and scoped credentials from MCP server
Server exposes permitted CRM and search connections, with explicit access limits
Four-step tool selection, execution, structured JSON result, model response
Reminder MCP is a protocol, not an authorization grant or a model
scenes.visual_example: get_opportunity(accountName: Acme Corp) returns a sample CRM opportunity Acme Expansion in Proposal stage, amount 250000 and close date 2025-04-30.
scenes.visual_synthesis: MCP standardizes tool discovery and calling, while authentication, authorization and system permissions remain separate responsibilities.
scenes.narration: This picture explains how an AI agent can use an external business system through MCP, the Model Context Protocol. MCP is a connection protocol, not an AI model or a permission grant. Begin on the left: a user asks for the latest opportunity for Acme Corp. Inside the agent application, an MCP client connects to an MCP server in the middle. The server describes available tools with a schema, meaning a named operation and its expected inputs and outputs. Its credentials must be scoped to approved actions. Follow the colored lines to the right: a CRM API can read authorized opportunities, while a search API can query allowed domains. Neither connection grants access to every account or website. The lower four boxes show one actual call. First the model selects get_opportunity and supplies the accountName Acme Corp. Second, the application sends the request via its MCP client to the server, which invokes the permitted CRM API. Third, the structured result returns with an illustrative opportunity ID, Acme Expansion, Proposal stage, a value of two hundred fifty thousand dollars and an April thirtieth, twenty twenty-five closing date. Finally, the model turns those fields into a readable response. The whole design separates choosing a tool from executing it and enforcing access. MCP helps interoperability, while the application and external service still enforce security.

scenes.title: Agent memory
scenes.visual_overview: A research agent gathers current knowledge, remembers only consented durable preferences and hands a structured result to a communications agent.
visual_walkthrough: Agent A asks for latest S3 pricing and a teammate summary
Three memory categories: temporary session state, approved persistent user preferences and retrieved company knowledge
Only approved preference enters durable storage; entire transcript is not automatically persisted
Agent B receives a structured pricing summary and sources
Consent, retention and authorized access boundaries; bottom three-stage worked example
scenes.visual_example: Agent A finds S3 pricing information and saves only the preference 'I prefer concise bullet points' with approval, then sends the summary, sources and confidence to Agent B.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Memory maintains continuity and agent handoffs, but every memory access remains subject to privacy, retention and permissions.
scenes.narration: The goal of this slide is to show what an AI agent should remember and what it should not. Start on the left with Agent A, a research assistant asked to find current Amazon S3 pricing and summarize it for a teammate. The three middle columns represent different kinds of information. Session context is temporary working state such as the current goal, recent messages and intermediate results. Persistent memory stores approved preferences, such as how a person likes responses formatted, across future sessions. Retrieved knowledge is different: it is company documentation or other relevant reference material fetched when needed, not a permanent memory of the person. Follow the downward arrow from persistent preferences into durable memory storage. The picture deliberately warns against storing an entire unfiltered conversation transcript; in the example only the approved preference for concise bullet points is saved. Follow the right arrow to Agent B, the communications assistant. It receives a structured result containing an S3 pricing summary, key points, sources and a confidence indication, then prepares the teammate message. The bottom worked example repeats those three stages. Finally, read the access boundary box: obtain consent, define how long to keep the information, and restrict who or which agent can access it. Memory can improve continuity, but it never overrides a person's permissions or makes old information automatically current.
